## Leviticus 22 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Overview of the Chapter

**Traditional Outline:**

The chapter falls into two main sections: (A) vv.1–16 — regulations about who may eat the holy offerings and in what state of purity; (B) vv.17–33 — regulations about the quality and condition of animals brought for sacrifice. (Gill, biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/22.htm; Matthew Henry, biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/leviticus/22.htm)

Guzik summarizes it as "More Specific Instructions for Priests," noting that the priests were to treat holy things with careful respect, could be restored after uncleanness by washing and waiting until evening (a picture of new mercies each morning), and that only perfect, unblemished offerings were acceptable — foreshadowing Christ. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-22/)

Dr. Constable notes the chapter contains twenty-eight selected laws (7 × 4) in four groups of seven, governing what profanes a priest (vv.1–9), who may eat sacred offerings (vv.10–16), acceptable animals (vv.17–25), and time intervals for sacrifices (vv.26–33). (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/leviticus-22.html)

---

### Verses 1–3: The Need for Ceremonial Purity

**v. 1 — "Then the LORD said to Moses"**

A standard formula introducing divine legislation. Gill notes this was "immediately after he had spoken concerning blemishes in priests, and in a continued discourse" — meaning that though priests with physical blemishes could eat the holy things (ch. 21), even unblemished priests under ceremonial impurity could not. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/22.htm)

**v. 2 — "Tell Aaron and his sons to treat with respect the sacred offerings..."**

The Hebrew verb translated "separate themselves from" (BSB: "treat with respect") is cognate to the noun *nazir* ("Nazirite"), carrying the connotation "to put away for separate use" or "treat as distinct." (Guzik, citing Rooker; enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-22/)

Ellicott explains the priests are warned that they are not absolutely entitled to the holy portions under all circumstances — there are times they must abstain. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/22.htm)

The Catholic Haydock commentary notes this is about behaving with great reverence in sacred offices, lest others take occasion to treat God's name with disrespect. It cites St. Basil: such consecrated things must not be used for ordinary purposes. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/leviticus-22.html)

Matthew Henry notes that "the holy things were their livelihood; if they might not eat of them, how must they subsist?" — thus the law was a strong incentive to preserve purity. (biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/leviticus/22.htm)

**v. 3 — "if any of their descendants in a state of uncleanness approaches the sacred offerings...that person must be cut off from My presence"**

The phrase "cut off from My presence" is a unique form of the excision penalty. Ellicott observes this exact wording ("from My presence") does not occur elsewhere in the Pentateuch for the excision formula (normally "cut off from his people"). The exceptional form may refer to the peculiar circumstances: if a priest presumptuously approaches in defilement, God Himself will banish him as He did Nadab and Abihu. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/22.htm)

Guzik, citing Peter-Contesse, explains "cut off from My presence" means no longer allowed to serve God — the expression contrasts with "to stand before someone," which means to serve. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-22/)

Catholic reading (Challoner, cited in Haydock): this teaches "with what purity of soul we are to approach to the blessed sacrament, of which these meats that had been offered in sacrifice were a figure." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/leviticus-22.html)

---

### Verses 4–8: Specific Causes of Defilement

**v. 4 — "If a descendant of Aaron has a skin disease or a discharge, he may not eat the sacred offerings until he is clean..."**

The leper (skin disease) and the person with a discharge (see Lev 13 and 15) represent more lasting defilements. Gill notes that even the wives and daughters of priests, if in these conditions, were excluded until cleansed. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/22.htm)

The Catholic Haydock, following Calmet, draws a noteworthy inference: "Hence it is plain, even the Jewish priests were bound to observe continence during the time of their ministry. For the same reason, the priests of the new law, who may be called at any time to perform their more sacred functions, engage voluntarily in the state of perpetual celibacy." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/leviticus-22.html)

Defilement by a corpse and emission of semen are also listed. Matthew Henry observes that some pollutions were permanent (leprosy, discharge) — "These separated the people from the sanctuary, and God would show that they were so far from being more excusable that really they were more abominable in a priest." (biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/leviticus/22.htm)

**v. 5 — "whoever touches a crawling creature or a person that makes him unclean"**

Crawling creatures (see Lev 11:24–44) and contact with an unclean person (a leper or someone with a discharge, Lev 15:5ff) are specified. Jarchi (cited by Gill) notes the phrase "whatsoever uncleanness he hath" includes touching a profluvious man or woman, a menstruous woman, and a new mother. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/22.htm)

**v. 6 — "the man who touches any of these will remain unclean until evening. He must not eat from the sacred offerings unless he has bathed himself with water."**

The cleansing ritual: washing and waiting until evening. Guzik sees this as a spiritual picture: "No matter how we might have failed the day before, we can begin each new day pure and close to the LORD. His mercies are new every morning (Lamentations 3:23)." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-22/)

Gill adds an interesting New Testament application from the Targum of Jonathan: "yea, when the evening is come, he may not eat of the heave or wave offerings, until he has dipped himself all over in water; nor should any eat of the Lord's supper under the New Testament, but such as are first baptized in water." (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/22.htm)

**v. 7 — "When the sun has set, he will become clean, and then he may eat from the sacred offerings, for they are his food."**

The Jewish day begins at sundown. Gill explains the compassionate reasoning: "because it is his food — his common food, his ordinary diet...this being his only substance, in compassion to him they were detained from him no longer than the evening; and this was done, to make him careful how he defiled himself, since thereby he was debarred of his ordinary meals." (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/22.htm)

**v. 8 — "He must not eat anything found dead or torn by wild animals, which would make him unclean."**

This restates a law already given to all Israel (Lev 17:15–16), now emphasized for priests. Gill notes: "these things were forbid a common Israelite, and much less might a priest eat of them." (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/22.htm)

---

### Verse 9: Summary Warning

**v. 9 — "The priests must keep My charge, lest they bear the guilt and die because they profane it. I am the LORD who sanctifies them."**

Guzik comments: "This more severe punishment for the willful ritual uncleanness of the priests was appropriate considering their greater knowledge of the things of God and their greater responsibility." He who is given more will be accountable for more (Luke 12:47–48). (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-22/)

Matthew Henry: "Sin is a burden which, if infinite mercy prevent not, will certainly sink those that bear it: They shall die therefore. Even priests may be ruined by their pollutions and presumptions." (biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/leviticus/22.htm)

---

### Verses 10–13: Who May Eat the Holy Offerings

**v. 10 — "No one outside a priest's family may eat the sacred offering, nor may the guest of a priest or his hired hand eat it."**

The principle: the sacred food is for the priest's permanent household only. Guzik notes this "went somewhat against the strong custom of hospitality in that culture, which normally insisted on giving guests the very best the home had to offer." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-22/)

"Outsider" (Hebrew *zar*) can be rendered "layman" — one not of the seed of Aaron (Rooker, cited by Guzik). The Pulpit Commentary homiletics applies this spiritually: "No mere casual guest, or even a hired servant of a priest's, was to eat of the holy things...Only those who enter on it with whole hearts, who dedicate themselves to it, body, soul, and spirit, need expect to participate in its privileges." (biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/leviticus/22.htm)

Matthew Henry sees a gospel parallel: "Those only are entitled to the comforts of God's house who make it their rest for ever, and resolve to dwell in it all the days of their life. As for those who for a time only believe, to serve a present turn, they are looked upon but as sojourners and mercenaries, and have no part nor lot in the matter." (biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/leviticus/22.htm)

**v. 11 — "But if a priest buys a slave with his own money, or if a slave is born in his household, that slave may eat his food."**

A purchased slave or one born in the household was considered permanent family, unlike a hired hand. Guzik, citing Adam Clarke, notes: "We see that it was lawful, under the Mosaic economy, to have slaves under certain restrictions; but these were taken from among the heathen, and instructed in the true religion...they were reckoned as a part of the priest's own family, and treated as such." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-22/)

**The Spurgeon connection (Baptist):** The Biblical Illustrator records Spurgeon's spiritual application: "Two classes were free at the sacred table — those who were bought with the priest's money, and those who were born into the priest's house." Spurgeon applies this to Christ: "Our great High Priest has bought with a price all those who put their trust in Him...'Because ye belong to Christ,' therefore shall ye share with your Lord." And of the second: "Regeneration makes us fellow-heirs...the peace, the joy, the glory, which the Father has given to Christ, Christ has given to us." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/leviticus-22.html, search excerpt)

**v. 12 — "If the priest's daughter is married to a man other than a priest, she is not to eat of the sacred contributions."**

By marrying outside the priestly line, she transfers to another family and loses her right. Gill explains: "being removed into another family by marriage, she is not reckoned of her father's family." (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/22.htm)

**v. 13 — "But if a priest's daughter with no children becomes widowed or divorced and returns to her father's house, she may share her father's food as in her youth."**

The condition "no children" is crucial — if she had a child (especially a son) by a non-priest, she would belong to that child's family. Guzik, citing Rooker: "The daughter would have the legal status she had before marriage, living under her father's roof and dependent on her father for her livelihood." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-22/)

A New Testament parallel noted: "the holiness of a priest extended throughout his household. A New Testament parallel pertains to those who reside in the home of believer priests (1 Corinthians 7:14)." (Rooker, cited by Guzik)

The Haydock Catholic commentary, citing Philo, adds: "If she had any [children], she remained with them." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/leviticus-22.html)

---

### Verses 14–16: Restitution for Accidental Eating

**v. 14 — "If anyone eats a sacred offering in error, he must add a fifth to its value and give the sacred offering to the priest."**

This follows the pattern of the trespass offering (Lev 5:16; 6:5). Guzik, citing Trapp: "All the water in Jordan, and the ceremonies in Leviticus, cannot cleanse a man so long as the polluted thing remains in his hand." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-22/)

Haydock notes: if someone ate deliberately (presumptuously), he was to be slain (Numbers 15:30); the restitution with a fifth is only for unintentional eating. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/leviticus-22.html)

**v. 15 — "The priests must not profane the sacred offerings that the Israelites present to the LORD"**

The priests are charged with guarding the offerings from misuse. The Catholic Haydock reads the subject as "the common people shall not profane, by touching them afterwards, or by retaining any part" — but adds: "The priests shall answer for the profanation, if it be committed through their neglect." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/leviticus-22.html)

**v. 16 — "by allowing the people to eat the sacred offerings and thus to bear the punishment for guilt."**

Matthew Henry interprets this two ways: (1) the priests must not cause lay people to incur guilt by permitting them to eat; (2) alternatively, the priests' eating of sin-offerings signified "bearing the iniquity of the congregation" (Lev 10:17), so a stranger must not presume to do what only appointed priests could do. He adds: "Those that set up other mediators besides Christ our priest, to bear the iniquity of trespass, sacrilegiously rob Christ of his honour." (biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/leviticus/22.htm)

---

### Verses 17–21: Offerings Must Be Without Blemish

**vv. 17–18 — God addresses not just priests but "all the Israelites" and "any foreign resident"**

This section broadens to include all who would bring offerings. Gill notes that "strangers in Israel" includes proselytes of the gate and proselytes of righteousness. Maimonides (cited by Gill) records the rabbinic rule that Gentiles could bring burnt offerings but not peace offerings — because peace offerings were eaten by Israelites, while burnt offerings were wholly devoted to God. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/22.htm)

**v. 19 — "must offer an unblemished male from the cattle, sheep, or goats"**

For a burnt offering, a male without defect is required. Guzik, citing Poole, notes: "A male for a burnt-offering, which was always of that kind; but the females were accepted in peace-offerings (Lev 3:1) and sin-offerings (Lev 4:32, 5:6)." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-22/)

**v. 20 — "You must not present anything with a defect, because it will not be accepted on your behalf."**

Guzik calls this God's standard of "perfect." He applies it Christologically: "Jesus was perfect in His nature as both God and man...in His motives...in His attitude...in His obedience...in His sacrifice for sin on our behalf." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-22/)

Matthew Henry connects it to Malachi 1:7–8, where God rebukes those who offered blind, lame, and sick animals. "Offer it then to your governor! Would he be pleased with you?" — the point being that people showed more respect to human rulers than to God. (biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/leviticus/22.htm)

The Baptist Garner-Howes Commentary applies it three ways: this typifies (1) Christ the perfect sacrifice (Isa 53; John 1:29; 1 Cor 5:7); (2) the "perfect heart" God requires (Ps 24:3–5); (3) God requiring the very best of all His child has. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/leviticus-22.html)

**v. 21 — "When a man presents a peace offering...it must be without blemish or defect to be acceptable."**

The same standard applies to peace offerings (whether for a vow or freewill). The Hebrew word translated "perfect" (*tamim*) means "complete, whole, sound, unimpaired" — the opposite of "defective." (Peter-Contesse, cited by Guzik; enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-22/)

---

### Verses 22–25: Specific Blemishes Listed

**v. 22 — "blind, injured, or maimed, or anything with a running sore, a festering rash, or a scab"**

Six specific defects. Guzik notes it is "not easy to identify the meaning of each of these with certainty" but the general principle is clear. He applies it to the believer's living sacrifice (Rom 12:1–2): our sacrifice should not be blind (eyes open to God's glory), broken (whole and complete), maimed (ready to serve), or with ulcers/scabs (diseased and troubled flesh evident to all). (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-22/)

**The Spurgeon/Baptist application** (from The Biblical Illustrator) is extensive. Spurgeon preached that just as blemished animals were excluded, so self-righteousness is excluded: "If you can come up to this rule you shall be saved by your righteousness; but if you cannot reach you must fail of acceptance." The rule "shuts us up to the sacrifice of Jesus Christ." He then applies each blemish to Christian service: not blind (serve with a single eye to God's glory), not broken (serve with the whole being), not maimed (not grudgingly — "some people give...with a limp"), not having a wen (avoid "that big wen of pride"), not scabbed (avoid irritable temper while trying to be benevolent). (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/leviticus-22.html)

**v. 23 — "You may present as a freewill offering an ox or sheep that has a deformed or stunted limb, but it is not acceptable in fulfillment of a vow."**

A significant distinction: deformed/stunted limbs (disproportionately long or short members) disqualified an animal for a vow offering but permitted it for a freewill offering. The Haydock commentary, citing Bochart and the Rabbins, explains the Hebrew *saruang* as animals whose "double members, feet, ears, etc., are disproportionately long," while *kalut* means too short. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/leviticus-22.html)

The Pulpit Commentary Homiletics sees this as encouragement: "God does not insist on the absolute perfection of the work of his people. If it is willing (verse 23) — if it is really a 'freewill offering' — then God will accept it in the spirit in which it is given." (biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/leviticus/22.htm)

Matthew Henry draws a practical lesson about vows: "God would teach us to make conscience of performing our promises to him very exactly, and not afterwards to abate in quantity or value of what we had solemnly engaged to devote to him. What was, before the vow, in our own power, as in the case of a free-will offering, afterwards is not (Acts 5:4)." (biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/leviticus/22.htm)

**v. 24 — "You are not to present to the LORD an animal whose testicles are bruised, crushed, torn, or cut"**

The reference is to castration. The Cambridge Bible states plainly: "A reference to emasculation. Animals thus treated were forbidden to be offered." (biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/leviticus/22.htm)

Guzik notes that the older NKJV translation obscures this: "The idea of castration is not clear in the New King James translation but is in many others...Most modern translations agree with this rendering." It didn't matter if castration was accidental or intentional. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-22/)

The Catholic Haydock, citing Josephus, extends the prohibition: "You shall not sacrifice any thing that is rendered unfit to propagate its kind: neither shall you reduce either man or beast to that condition." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/leviticus-22.html)

**v. 25 — "Neither you nor a foreigner shall present food to your God from any such animal."**

God would not accept defective sacrifices from anyone. Guzik explains: "If an Israelite bought a castrated animal from a foreigner's hand they could not offer it." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-22/)

Matthew Henry observes that even strangers "should be welcome" to bring offerings (1 Kgs 8:41–42; Ezra 6:9–10; Isa 56:6–7) but that "the God of Israel would not be so served" with blemished sacrifices — unlike heathen priests who "would receive sacrifices for their gods that were ever so scandalous." (biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/leviticus/22.htm)

---

### Verses 26–30: Time and Manner Regulations

**v. 27 — "When an ox, a sheep, or a goat is born, it must remain with its mother for seven days. From the eighth day on, it will be acceptable."**

This parallels Exodus 22:30. Matthew Henry notes the Jewish rationale: "It was because the sabbath sanctifies all things, and nothing should be offered to God till at least one sabbath had passed over it." He also sees a connection to circumcision on the eighth day and to Christ being sacrificed "not in his infancy...but in the prime of his time." (biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/leviticus/22.htm)

The Catholic Haydock, citing Tertullian, sees a lesson of humanity in this and the following verses. The Romans similarly did not offer sheep or goats before eight days; Jews generally waited until thirty days. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/leviticus-22.html)

Dr. Constable (Dallas Theological Seminary) notes: "It took these animals this long to attain the strength and maturity necessary for them to represent the offerer adequately." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/leviticus-22.html)

**v. 28 — "But you must not slaughter an ox or a sheep on the same day as its young."**

Guzik says this was "to imitate a Canaanite fertility ritual. This was forbidden to Israel." Citing Rooker: "These laws may have had a polemical function against pagan practices or they may merely promote sensitivities and high regard for life." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-22/)

Guzik also cites Adam Clarke: "The precept was certainly intended to inculcate mercy and tenderness of heart...When it is necessary to take away the lives of innocent animals for the support of our own, we should do it in such a way as not to blunt our moral feelings."

Matthew Henry calls it "barbarous and cruel to the brute creatures; like the tyranny of the king of Babylon, that slew Zedekiah's sons before his eyes, and then put out his eyes. It looked ill-natured towards the species to kill two generations at once, as if one designed the ruin of the kind." (biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/leviticus/22.htm)

Dr. Constable offers an alternative explanation: "this ruling simply conserved the animal stock that would have become depleted otherwise" (citing Wenham and Ross). (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/leviticus-22.html)

**v. 29 — "When you sacrifice a thank offering to the LORD, offer it so that it may be acceptable on your behalf."**

The phrase "offer it of your own free will" (NKJV) is key. Guzik explains: "When it came to an offering meant to show thanksgiving, God only wanted sincere gratitude. It had to come from the free will of the offerer." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-22/)

**v. 30 — "It must be eaten that same day. Do not leave any of it until morning."**

This repeats Lev 7:15. The thank offering's meat was to be consumed the same day — part to the LORD (burned), part to the priest, and the remainder for the offerer's household celebration. Guzik explains the practical concern: in an age without refrigeration, meat left overnight would spoil and become profane. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-22/)

---

### Verses 31–33: Concluding Exhortation

**v. 31 — "You are to keep My commandments and practice them. I am the LORD."**

Guzik summarizes the four reasons God gives Israel to obey:
- Because of *who God is* — "I am the LORD"
- Because of *what He is* — "My holy name"
- Because of *what He is doing* — "I am the LORD who sanctifies you"
- Because of *what He has done* — "who brought you out of the land of Egypt"
(enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-22/)

**v. 32 — "You must not profane My holy name. I must be acknowledged as holy among the Israelites."**

Guzik, citing Poole: "Neither shall ye profane my holy name; either by despising me and my command yourselves, or by giving others occasion to profane them." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-22/)

Matthew Henry warns: "Those that profess God's name, if they do not make conscience of keeping his commandments, do but profane his name." He adds that God "will be a loser in his glory by no man at last; but sooner or later will recover his right, either in the repentance of sinners or in their ruin." (biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/leviticus/22.htm)

**v. 33 — "who brought you out of the land of Egypt to be your God. I am the LORD."**

Guzik closes: "Because Yahweh (the LORD) was the God of Israel, and because of all He had done for them, their obedience to Him was proper. These same reasons remain true for every believer today." He quotes G. Campbell Morgan: "Jehovah is the God of holiness because He is essentially the God of love." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-22/)

---

## Distinctive Protestant Tradition Readings

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik)

Guzik emphasizes the present spiritual application of every detail. The washing-and-waiting ritual pictures how "His mercies are new every morning." The call for a "perfect" sacrifice is applied directly to the believer: "We should offer ourselves to God as living sacrifices — whole, not blind, not broken or maimed, without diseased or troubled flesh — holding back nothing from Him." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-22/)

### Baptist (Spurgeon / The Biblical Illustrator)

Spurgeon's reading of vv.10–13 is distinctively Christ-centered and soteriological: the two classes who may eat — those bought with the priest's money and those born in his house — are "bought" (redemption) and "born" (regeneration). He presses the "perfect" requirement of v.21 to exclude all self-righteousness and drive sinners to Christ alone. His application of the blemishes (v.22) to the manner of Christian service — blind, broken, maimed, scabbed service — is a characteristic Baptist emphasis on wholehearted devotion. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/leviticus-22.html)

### Reformed (Matthew Henry)

Matthew Henry consistently draws the connection between the ceremonial law and the holiness of God, emphasizing human inability and the need for Christ. His reading of v.16 — that the priest "bearing iniquity" points to Christ as the sole mediator — is a Reformed distinctive: "Those that set up other mediators besides Christ our priest, to bear the iniquity of trespass, sacrilegiously rob Christ of his honour, and invade his rights." (biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/leviticus/22.htm)

### Brethren / Plymouth Brethren (Grant's Commentary)

Grant (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/leviticus-22.html) emphasizes that even freewill offerings must be without blemish — "for some might think that, though the compulsory offerings for sin and trespass must be without defect, yet this might not be required if the offering was giving voluntarily. But the burnt offering was offered primarily for God's glory, and no defect was to be allowed." This reflects the Brethren emphasis on God's glory as the primary purpose of worship.

---

## Other Views

### Catholic (Haydock, 1811)

Catholic reading finds distinctively Catholic applications:
- **v.3:** The sacred food prefigures the Blessed Sacrament, teaching "with what purity of soul we are to approach" it (Challoner).
- **v.4:** The requirement of ritual purity for priests supports the discipline of clerical celibacy: "For the same reason, the priests of the new law, who may be called at any time to perform their more sacred functions, engage voluntarily in the state of perpetual celibacy."
- **v.24:** The prohibition against castrated animals extends morally to humans: "neither shall you reduce either man or beast to that condition" (citing Josephus).
 (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/leviticus-22.html)

### Modern Scholarship (NET Bible notes, Cambridge Bible)

The Cambridge Bible for Schools and Colleges notes the chapter's composite nature: "The whole or part of Leviticus 22:1–2 may be looked upon as the introductory formula by Rp [a Reviser who introduced further elements from the Priestly Code]." (biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/leviticus/22.htm)

Dr. Constable (Dallas Theological Seminary, evangelical) sees the chapter as structured in four groups of seven laws (28 total, 7 × 4). He notes alternative explanations for v.28 (not killing mother and young on the same day): Keil and Delitzsch suggest it was "to keep sacred the relation which God had established between parent and offspring," while Wenham and Ross suggest it "simply conserved the animal stock." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/leviticus-22.html)

The Bridgeway Commentary suggests the freewill offering exception (v.23) is because "the state of the animal was an indication of the offerer's state of heart." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/leviticus-22.html)

### Summary of Unavailable Traditions

Due to search limitations, I was unable to locate chapter-specific Leviticus 22 commentaries from the following approved sites: **ligonier.org, thegospelcoalition.org** (Reformed); **lcms.org, 1517.org** (Lutheran); **desiringGod.org** (John Piper/Baptist-Reformed); **seedbed.com, wesley.nnu.edu** (Methodist/Wesleyan); **samstorms.org, pneumareview.com, ag.org** (Pentecostal beyond Guzik); **oca.org** (Orthodox); **bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org** (modern scholarship beyond Cambridge); **catholic.com** (Catholic beyond Haydock). References to these traditions above are drawn from what Guzik, Gill, Matthew Henry, and the Biblical Illustrator report of their views, or from general principles evident in the sources examined.
